assumptions: Assumes an observer of the flow, or an intermediary with access to traffic metadata, can correlate repeated transmissions over time.

description: When processing the parent's invitation, the backend may not clearly inform the parent about the exact data that the secondary guardian will gain access to, the duration of access, whether precise live location is included, and whether the child or other guardians will be notified. Lack of clear notice undermines informed privacy decisions.
assumptions: The backend controls invitation UX/content or API behavior that determines what notice is presented.
uncertainty_note: Applies if notice is incomplete or ambiguous; exact UI details are not provided.

title: Backend may lack sufficient evidence of who initiated the invitation and what scope was granted
description: If the backend does not retain trustworthy records of the invitation request, the parent could later deny having invited the secondary guardian, or the service may be unable to prove what access scope and timing were authorized. This impairs accountability for a sensitive sharing action involving a child's location.
assumptions: Audit trails for invitation initiation, recipient, scope, and timestamps may be incomplete or mutable.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation is included in LINDDUN, but whether this is a privacy threat in scope can depend on the project's interpretation.

title: Backend discloses the child's live location to a secondary guardian without sufficient authorization or necessity checks
description: The source process shares highly sensitive real-time location data with EE3. If the backend grants access without verifying the secondary guardian's legitimacy, current authorization status, or the child's/primary guardian's configured permissions, it may disclose personal data to an unintended or no-longer-authorized recipient.
assumptions: Assumes secondary-guardian relationships can change over time and that live location is sensitive personal data requiring explicit authorization checks before each grant/share action.

title: Live-location data in transit can identify the child and guardian relationship
description: The data flow carries real-time location information from the backend to the secondary guardian. Even if the payload is limited, the transmitted location and associated account/session metadata can identify the child and reveal that EE3 is connected to that child as a guardian.
assumptions: Assumes the flow includes or is accompanied by identifiers, session tokens, routing metadata, or stable account context sufficient to associate the location with a specific child or household.
uncertainty_note: Exact identification node may vary depending on the project's threat-tree granularity.

title: Repeated live-location updates enable linkability of the child's movements over time
description: Because the backend shares live location, successive messages on this flow can be linked together to build a movement history for the same child. This allows correlation of visits, routines, and co-location patterns across time.
assumptions: Assumes the flow is recurring or continuous and that updates are associated with the same child/session over time.

title: Secondary guardian may further disclose or misuse the child's live location after receipt
description: Once EE3 receives the child's live location, the destination party may store, screenshot, forward, or verbally share it beyond the intended purpose. This creates an onward-disclosure risk outside the original sharing context.
assumptions: Assumes EE3 is an external entity outside direct technical control of the system and may have means to retain or redistribute the received location data.
uncertainty_note: This is a destination-side disclosure threat grounded in recipient behavior; exact node id is best-effort.

title: Backend may share live location without valid consent or another appropriate legal basis
description: Granting a secondary guardian access to a child's live location may require explicit consent, parental authorization, or another valid legal basis depending on jurisdiction and custody context. If the backend performs the share without recording and enforcing that basis, the processing may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes the system is subject to privacy/data-protection obligations and that child live-location sharing is regulated or requires documented authorization.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and product context; exact legal basis requirements may vary.

title: The backend may not provide sufficient transparency about live-location sharing to the affected parties
description: If the system grants EE3 access and shares the child's live location without clearly informing the child’s responsible parties about who receives access, when sharing starts, and under what conditions, the processing may be insufficiently transparent.
assumptions: Assumes transparency notices, in-app indicators, or audit visibility may be absent or incomplete for this sharing event.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on whether the product already provides clear notices and sharing indicators.

title: Insufficient evidence of the grant/share action can undermine accountability for location sharing
description: If the backend does not log who granted EE3 access, when the live location was shared, and under which authorization context, parties may later be unable to prove or dispute that the disclosure occurred appropriately. This weakens accountability for a sensitive sharing action.
assumptions: Assumes audit logging or tamper-evident records for access grants and disclosures may be missing or incomplete.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation in privacy threat modeling is sometimes interpreted differently across LINDDUN materials; node id is best-effort.

title: Backend disclosure of analytics to third-party partner may exceed user expectations
description: By sending usage and engagement analytics to an advertising/analytics partner to fund the free tier, the backend discloses information about users' behavior to a separate organization. Even if described as aggregated, the act of sharing can reveal information about cohorts or segments and may go beyond what users reasonably expect from core app functionality.
assumptions: The shared analytics are derived from user behavior and are not purely anonymous in a mathematically robust sense.

title: Partner may link received analytics with its existing datasets
description: The advertising/analytics partner may combine the received aggregated usage and engagement analytics with other datasets it already holds, enabling linkage across apps, campaigns, regions, time windows, or audience segments. This can increase the ability to single out or profile groups and, in some cases, infer information about individuals if aggregates are small or repeatedly shared.
assumptions: EE4 operates across multiple clients or data sources and has incentives and technical means to correlate incoming analytics with other data.
uncertainty_note: Applies most strongly if the aggregates are granular by time, geography, campaign, device type, or other dimensions.

title: Aggregated analytics may still enable inference of user or cohort identity
description: If the shared analytics contain small-cell counts, rare-event metrics, or fine-grained segment breakdowns, the recipient may infer the identity of a user, household, or narrowly defined cohort from the data, especially when combined with auxiliary information.
assumptions: Aggregation thresholds, suppression, or differential privacy are absent or weak.
uncertainty_note: This depends heavily on how coarse the aggregation really is.

title: Recipient processing may disclose sensitive behavioral insights
description: On receipt, the partner can analyze the engagement data to derive and expose sensitive insights about user populations, such as interests, habits, or potentially vulnerable segments, even if raw identifiers are absent. Such derived disclosures can affect users through targeting or downstream sharing.
assumptions: Usage and engagement metrics correlate with meaningful behavioral traits or sensitive interests.
uncertainty_note: Threat is stronger where app usage patterns are sensitive by nature.

title: Secondary use by partner for advertising or model improvement may be unaware to users
description: Users may be unaware that their app-derived analytics are shared with an external advertising/analytics partner and then used for purposes beyond funding analytics reporting, such as ad targeting, audience modeling, benchmarking, or product improvement.
assumptions: Not all downstream purposes are clearly communicated to users at collection time.
uncertainty_note: If notices and in-product disclosures are explicit and prominent, this threat may be reduced but not eliminated.

title: Sharing with advertising partner may lack valid consent or other lawful basis
description: Transferring usage and engagement analytics to an advertising/analytics partner for monetization may require consent or another valid legal basis, especially where the data supports advertising, profiling, or cross-context analytics. If the partner's purposes are not adequately covered, the processing may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Applicable law or platform policy treats this sharing as requiring consent, opt-out, or specific transparency obligations.
uncertainty_note: Legal applicability depends on jurisdiction, platform rules, and whether the data is truly anonymized.

title: Child discloses precise real-time location and SOS status
description: By sending a manual check-in or SOS message with current location, the child reveals highly sensitive contextual information (precise whereabouts and possible distress state) to the system. This creates a privacy threat because the act of sharing exposes more personal information than may be strictly necessary for all situations, especially if precision, frequency, or message content are not minimized.

title: Location-bearing message can link repeated check-ins to the same child
description: The data flow carries identifiers and/or stable communication metadata that can allow repeated manual check-ins or SOS events to be linked to the same child over time. Even if message content were partly protected, timing, routing, account, device, or session metadata may enable correlation of the child's movements and behavior patterns.
assumptions: The backend can associate the message with a child account, device, session, or other persistent identifier.

title: Message and metadata may identify the child in transit
description: The check-in/SOS message likely contains direct or indirect identifiers such as account identifiers, device identifiers, network metadata, and precise location. In transit, these data can identify the child or make them identifiable to parties able to observe or access the communication path.

title: SOS/check-in message becomes attributable evidence of the child's action
description: The manual message can serve as evidence that this specific child initiated a check-in or SOS at a particular time and place. This may reduce the child's ability to later deny having sent the message, especially if the backend records account, device, timestamp, and location together.
assumptions: The backend logs the message with identifiers, timestamps, and location in a way that preserves attribution.

title: Backend may expose sensitive location and distress data beyond the immediate purpose
description: Upon receipt, the backend may store, analyze, or redistribute the child's location and SOS/check-in content in ways that disclose sensitive information beyond what is necessary to notify the parent. Examples include retaining detailed history, making data accessible to operators, or using it for analytics or secondary purposes.
assumptions: The backend stores or processes the received message rather than acting only as an ephemeral relay.

title: Backend can infer behavior patterns and sensitive situations from repeated check-ins
description: By collecting repeated manual check-ins and SOS messages with timestamps and locations, the backend can derive additional personal information not explicitly provided, such as routines, school/home locations, social patterns, emergencies, or periods of vulnerability.
assumptions: The backend retains multiple events over time and can correlate them per child.

title: Child may be unaware of backend retention and secondary processing
description: The child may not understand how long the backend keeps SOS/check-in messages, who can access them, whether precise location is mandatory, or whether the data are reused for analytics, safety scoring, or operational monitoring. This creates a privacy threat if processing is insufficiently transparent to the child.
assumptions: The child is a data subject with limited visibility into backend processing and retention practices.

title: Processing a child's precise location and SOS data may exceed valid consent or child-specific legal basis
description: The backend's receipt and processing of a child's precise location and distress-related message may require explicit parental authorization, child-appropriate notices, purpose limitation, and special protections. If these are absent or insufficient, the processing may be non-compliant with child-data and location-data requirements.
